title: Chapter 00–01: Unix Environment & Java Toolchain Setup
description: Build a rock-solid Unix development environment—understanding WSL2 filesystem boundaries, essential terminal navigation, Git identity, SDKMAN!, Java 25 LTS, and Maven.

sources.title: DAI Chapter 00: Environment Setup
sources.notes: Unix environment (Linux, macOS, WSL2), terminal basics, Git, SDKMAN!, Java 25 LTS, and Maven.

sections.title: 1. Unix Shell & WSL2 Filesystem Architecture
sections.description: Understand why network programming relies on a real Unix shell and how WSL2 separates native Linux storage from the Windows filesystem.

blocks.title: Why a Real Unix Shell Matters
blocks.content:
Networked applications and containers run overwhelmingly on Unix-like systems. Working inside a real Unix shell ensures your file permissions, line endings (`LF` vs `CRLF`), symlinks, and tooling behave identically to production Linux servers and Docker containers.

- **Linux:** Native Unix shell and system package manager (`apt`, `dnf`, etc.).
- **macOS:** Native BSD/Unix shell (`zsh`/`bash`) paired with a package manager such as Homebrew.
- **Windows:** **WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux)** running a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM (e.g., Ubuntu LTS).

> **Non-Example:** Compatibility shims like Git Bash, Cygwin, or MSYS2 translate POSIX calls onto Windows and diverge from real Linux behavior on permissions, sockets, and container tooling. Always use a genuine Unix environment.

blocks.title: WSL2 Filesystem Boundaries: /home vs /mnt/c
blocks.content:
In WSL2, Windows and Linux each own a separate filesystem, connected by a cross-OS bridge:

1. **Native Linux Home (`~` / `/home/<user>`):** Lives on WSL2's virtual `ext4` disk. File I/O is fast and POSIX permissions (`chmod`, symlinks, executable bits) work natively. **All development projects must live here.**
2. **Windows Drives from Linux (`/mnt/c/`, `/mnt/d/`, …):** Windows NTFS drives mounted into Linux via the **9P protocol**. Crossing this bridge for builds (`mvn`, `git`, `docker`) causes severe I/O slowdowns, permission mismatches, and `CRLF` line-ending bugs.
3. **Linux Files from Windows (`\\wsl.localhost\<Distro>\home\<user>`):** Exposes the WSL2 filesystem to Windows tools (such as your IDE).

> **Caution:** Never manipulate files inside `/home/<user>` using Windows File Explorer or store projects on `C:\`. Run file operations (`mkdir`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `git`) inside the Unix terminal.

blocks.title: WSL2 vs Windows Filesystem Architecture
blocks.caption: Keep all projects inside the native Linux filesystem (/home/<user>) to avoid 9P bridge bottlenecks and POSIX permission corruption.

sections.title: 2. Unix Terminal Fundamentals & Git Identity
sections.description: Build fluency with Unix paths and core shell commands, and configure Git cleanly.

blocks.title: Paths & Essential Unix Terminal Commands
blocks.content:
Unix paths are case-sensitive and separated by forward slashes (`/`). Key path anchors:
- `/` — filesystem root
- `~` — your home directory (`/home/<user>` on Linux, `/Users/<user>` on macOS)
- `.` — current directory
- `..` — parent directory

Use `man <command>` to inspect any command's manual.

| Command | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `pwd` | Print the current working directory |
| `ls` / `ls -la` | List files (`-l` long format, `-a` include hidden `.` files) |
| `cd <dir>` / `cd ..` | Change directory / move to parent directory |
| `touch <file>` | Create an empty file (or update its timestamp) |
| `mkdir -p <dir/sub>` | Create a directory (and missing parents with `-p`) |
| `rm <file>` / `rm -r <dir>` | Remove a file / recursively remove a directory |
| `cp <src> <dst>` | Copy a file (add `-r` for directories) |
| `mv <src> <dst>` | Move or rename a file/directory |
| `cat <file>` | Print the entire contents of a file |
| `less <file>` | Page through a file (`q` to quit) |
| `tail -f <file>` | Print the last lines and follow live log output |

blocks.title: Practice: WSL2 Path Safety Validator
blocks.instructions: Write a Python function `is_safe_wsl_path(path)` that returns `True` if a project path is safely inside the Linux `/home/` directory (or uses `~`), and `False` if it is on a Windows mount (`/mnt/...`) or a Windows-style path (`C:\...` or `\\wsl.localhost\...`). Run the code to verify all test cases pass.
blocks.starter_code:
def is_safe_wsl_path(path: str) -> bool:
    # TODO: Return True only if path starts with '/home/' or '~'
    pass

tests = [
    ("/home/alice/dai-lab01", True),
    ("~/projects/smtp-client", True),
    ("/mnt/c/Users/alice/dai-lab01", False),
    ("C:\\Users\\alice\\dai-lab01", False),
]

for p, expected in tests:
    result = is_safe_wsl_path(p)
    assert result == expected, f"Failed for {p}: got {result}, expected {expected}"
print("All WSL2 path checks passed!")
hints: Check `path.startswith('/home/')` for absolute Linux home paths.
Also allow `path == '~'` or `path.startswith('~/')` for home shorthand.

blocks.title: Git Identity Configuration
blocks.content:
Verify Git is available in your Unix shell with `git --version`, then configure your global author identity. Git stamps this name and email onto every commit you create:

```bash
git config --global user.name "First-name Last-name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
```

> **Note:** `user.name` and `user.email` are only a plain-text metadata label, **not** cryptographic proof of authorship. Anyone can set any name/email in Git config; cryptographic verification requires SSH or GPG commit signing.

sections.title: 3. Java 25 LTS & Maven via SDKMAN!
sections.description: Manage JDK and Maven versions cleanly with SDKMAN! and verify your toolchain from the terminal.

blocks.title: Installing Java 25 LTS & Maven with SDKMAN!
blocks.content:
**SDKMAN!** manages Java toolchain versions cleanly, letting you install and switch between JDKs and build tools without manual `PATH` or `JAVA_HOME` edits.

1. Install SDKMAN! and open a new shell so its initialization script is loaded.
2. List available JDK distributions, install the latest **Temurin** LTS Java (Java 25 LTS), and install **Maven**:

```bash
sdk list java
sdk install java <version>-tem
sdk install maven
```

3. Verify all three tools in your Unix terminal:
   - `sdk version`
   - `java --version` (should show Temurin 25 or newer LTS)
   - `mvn --version` (should show Maven bound to that same Java runtime)

blocks.title: Toolchain Verification Script
blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
pwd
git --version
git config user.name
sdk version
java --version
mvn --version

annotations.note: Confirms your current directory is inside your native Unix home (/home/<user> on Linux/WSL), not /mnt/c/.
Confirms your global Git commit author label is configured.
Must report Temurin 25 (or newer LTS) managed by SDKMAN!.
Verifies Maven is installed and bound to the same Java 25 runtime.

blocks.title: Synthesis: Diagnosing a Broken WSL2 Java Environment
blocks.prompt: A developer on Windows reports two issues: (1) their Maven builds are painfully slow and `chmod +x` has no effect because their repository is in `C:\Users\Alex\projects`, and (2) running `java --version` in Ubuntu prints 'command not found' even though they installed Java on Windows. Diagnose both issues and give the exact fixes.
self_check_criteria: Identified that storing projects on C:\ (/mnt/c/) crosses the 9P Windows-Linux filesystem boundary, causing slow I/O and broken POSIX permissions.
Specified moving the repository into the native Linux home directory (/home/<user> or ~) and running git/mvn commands from the Unix shell.
Explained that WSL2 is a separate Linux environment and does not automatically share Windows-installed JDKs.
Specified installing Java 25 LTS and Maven inside Ubuntu using SDKMAN! (`sdk install java <version>-tem`, `sdk install maven`) and verifying with `java --version` and `mvn --version`.
blocks.model_answer:
1) Storing projects in `C:\Users\Alex\projects` (`/mnt/c/...`) forces WSL2 to access files across the 9P Windows-Linux bridge, which causes severe I/O slowdowns for Maven/Git and prevents native POSIX permissions (`chmod`) from working properly. Move the repository into `/home/<user>/projects` inside WSL2 and manipulate files from the Ubuntu terminal.

2) WSL2 runs an isolated Linux userland, so a JDK installed on Windows is not your Linux `java` binary. Install SDKMAN! inside Ubuntu, then run `sdk install java <version>-tem` and `sdk install maven`. Open a new shell and verify with `java --version` and `mvn --version`.

blocks.target_audience: a first-year student who has only ever used Windows File Explorer
blocks.prompt: Explain in plain language why WSL2 has two separate file worlds (/home/<user> vs /mnt/c/), and why putting Java projects in C:\ or dragging files with Windows File Explorer causes trouble.
key_points_to_cover: WSL2 runs a real Linux computer inside Windows with its own native Linux disk (/home/<user>).
Accessing C:\ (/mnt/c/) or poking into Linux files from Windows Explorer forces two different operating systems to translate permissions and file formats across a slow bridge.
Keeping projects in /home/<user> and using only the Unix terminal (and opening the WSL path in an IDE) avoids permission corruption and slow builds.

sections.title: 4. Knowledge Retrieval & Spaced Repetition
sections.description: Test your mastery of WSL2 filesystem boundaries, Unix terminal navigation, Git identity, and SDKMAN! toolchain verification.

blocks.title: WSL2 Project Storage & File Access
blocks.question: On Windows with WSL2, where should you store your Java/network programming projects, and how should you manipulate those files?
options: Store them in `/home/<user>` (inside WSL) and manipulate them from the Ubuntu terminal (opening `\\wsl.localhost\...` in your IDE).
Store them in `C:\Users\<user>\Projects` (`/mnt/c/...`) so both Windows Explorer and Ubuntu can edit them freely.
Store them in `/home/<user>` and regularly organize or rename them using Windows File Explorer.
Use Git Bash on Windows so all files stay native to `C:\` without needing WSL2.
blocks.correct_answer: Store them in `/home/<user>` (inside WSL) and manipulate them from the Ubuntu terminal (opening `\\wsl.localhost\...` in your IDE).
blocks.explanation: All projects must live in the native Linux home directory (`/home/<user>`, shorthand `~`) to get fast ext4 I/O and real POSIX permissions. Storing projects under `/mnt/c/` forces traffic across the slow 9P bridge, while editing WSL files from Windows File Explorer causes permission corruption and line-ending issues. Git Bash is a Windows shim, not a real Linux environment.
hints: Think about which filesystem is native to the Ubuntu kernel where your builds and containers run.
Crossing the 9P bridge (`/mnt/c/`) or editing Linux files from Windows Explorer causes performance and permission bugs.

blocks.title: Print Working Directory Command
blocks.question: In a Unix terminal, the ___ command prints the full path of your current working directory.
blocks.explanation: `pwd` stands for 'print working directory' and outputs the absolute path of the folder your shell is currently in. `ls` lists directory contents, `cd` changes directories, and `cat` prints file contents.
hints: It is a 3-letter acronym for 'Print Working Directory'.
In Unix shells, it tells you where `cd` has currently placed you.

blocks.title: Predict Output: Unix Directory Navigation
blocks.question:
Suppose your shell starts in `/home/alice/projects/http-server`. What does `pwd` print after running the following commands?

```bash
cd ..
mkdir -p labs/lab01
cd labs/lab01
pwd
```
blocks.explanation:
`cd ..` moves up one level from `/home/alice/projects/http-server` to `/home/alice/projects`. `mkdir -p labs/lab01` creates `labs/lab01` inside `/home/alice/projects`, and `cd labs/lab01` enters it, so `pwd` prints `/home/alice/projects/labs/lab01`.

* `/home/alice/projects/http-server/labs/lab01` ignores the `cd ..` command.
* `/home/alice/labs/lab01` moves up two levels (`../..`) instead of one.
* `/labs/lab01` treats a relative path as an absolute path starting at `/`.
hints: `..` refers to the parent directory of the current working directory.
Paths without a leading `/` are relative to your current directory.

blocks.title: What Git's user.name and user.email Actually Prove
blocks.question: You run `git config --global user.name "Alice"` and `git config --global user.email "alice@example.com"`. What does this guarantee about commits you push?
options: Nothing cryptographically—it is only a plain-text label stamped onto commit metadata.
It cryptographically signs every commit with an SSH key.
GitHub verifies that you own `alice@example.com` before accepting any commit with that metadata.
It prevents anyone else from creating commits using the same name and email.
blocks.correct_answer: Nothing cryptographically—it is only a plain-text label stamped onto commit metadata.
blocks.explanation: Git's `user.name` and `user.email` are unverified metadata labels stored in `~/.gitconfig` and stamped into commit objects. Anyone can configure any name or email; cryptographic proof of authorship requires signing commits with SSH or GPG keys.
hints: Think about whether `git config` involves any private key or password.
Distinguish between commit metadata labels and cryptographic commit signing.

blocks.title: SDKMAN! & Java Toolchain Verification
blocks.question: Which statements about managing Java 25 LTS and Maven with SDKMAN! are **true**? (Select all that apply)
options: SDKMAN! manages `JAVA_HOME` and `PATH` for you so you can switch JDKs cleanly.
Running `mvn --version` confirms both Maven's version and the Java runtime it is using.
After installing SDKMAN!, you must open a new shell (or source its init script) before `sdk` commands work.
You must manually edit `/etc/environment` for every new JDK version installed via `sdk install java`.
correct_answer: SDKMAN! manages `JAVA_HOME` and `PATH` for you so you can switch JDKs cleanly.
Running `mvn --version` confirms both Maven's version and the Java runtime it is using.
After installing SDKMAN!, you must open a new shell (or source its init script) before `sdk` commands work.
blocks.explanation: SDKMAN! automatically manages `JAVA_HOME` and `PATH` via shell initialization scripts, which is why you open a new terminal after installing it. `mvn --version` outputs both the Maven version and the underlying Java version/vendor. Manual `/etc/environment` edits are unnecessary.
hints: Why do developers use SDKMAN! instead of manually configuring `JAVA_HOME`?
What information does `mvn --version` print besides Maven's own version?

blocks.title: WSL2 Home (~) vs Windows Mount (/mnt/c/)
blocks.front: In WSL2, what is the difference between `/home/<user>` (`~`) and `/mnt/c/`, and where must projects live?
blocks.back:
- **`/home/<user>` (`~`):** Native Linux `ext4` home directory inside WSL2. **All projects must live here.**
- **`/mnt/c/`:** Cross-OS 9P mount of your Windows `C:\` drive (slow I/O, broken POSIX permissions).
- Never edit WSL project files from Windows File Explorer (`\\wsl.localhost\...`).
blocks.hint: One is native Linux storage; the other crosses the 9P OS bridge.

blocks.title: SDKMAN! Java 25 LTS & Maven Commands
blocks.front: How do you list, install, and verify **Temurin Java 25 LTS** and **Maven** using **SDKMAN!**?
blocks.back:
1. `sdk list java` (find latest `<version>-tem` LTS)
2. `sdk install java <version>-tem`
3. `sdk install maven`
4. Verify with `sdk version`, `java --version`, and `mvn --version`.

blocks.title: Core Unix Terminal Commands
blocks.front: What do `pwd`, `touch`, `rm -r`, `cp -r`, `less`, and `tail -f` do in a Unix shell?
blocks.back:
- `pwd`: Print working directory
- `touch <file>`: Create empty file
- `rm -r <dir>`: Recursively delete directory
- `cp -r <src> <dst>`: Recursively copy directory
- `less <file>`: Page through file (`q` to quit)
- `tail -f <file>`: Follow live lines (e.g., logs)
blocks.hint: Basic file navigation, creation, deletion, and log inspection.

blocks.title: Git Global Identity Configuration
blocks.front: How do you set your Git author name and email globally, and is this a cryptographic proof of identity?
blocks.back:
```bash
git config --global user.name "First-name Last-name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
```
No—it is only an unverified **metadata label** stamped on commits. Cryptographic proof requires SSH or GPG commit signing.
